_: How the YouK range assembles, as data. Every number here was measured from
the meshes and cross-checked against Kesseboehmer's mounting instructions -
see FINDINGS.md. tools/add-snaps.py turns it into snap planes.
This file is the reviewable artefact. A wrong number here produces a model
that assembles confidently and incorrectly, so it is data in git rather than
_mask: ONE mask per ladder depth, shared by span and hang accessories, because a
rung mount is a rung mount: both families bolt through the same hole in the
same rung face. Giving them separate masks would mean two snaps at the same
point on the frame, and filling one would not fill the other - a shelf and a
tray could then occupy the same rung face. Depth is the axis that actually
gates compatibility, and it is already in the mask.
_rungTops: Height above the frame base of each rung member's TOP face, which is what an
accessory bears down on. Members are 4.9mm thick and start 95.1, 450.1,
805.1 ... above the base. A frame gets every rung whose top fits inside its
height - that rule reproduces the measured rung count on all six frames.
Depth 200 uses a 236.5mm pitch, depth 320 runs 355, 355, 595, 355, 355
between rung centres - the asymmetric-looking 595 is in Kesseboehmer's own
dimension chain and is confirmed in the geometry.
_mountHole: Every rung carries two 5x5mm holes in its top wall, at these distances
either side of the frame's depth centre. Each hang accessory carries a 9x6mm
obround slot over each of them. The two agree on both depths - 320 frames
and 320 accessories both use 95, 200s both use 35 - which is what proves a
hang accessory is centred on the frame's depth rather than offset.
add-snaps.py finds the slot by this number and takes the plug from it, so
the plug is measured from each part rather than typed in per part.
_frames: The ladder frames. Converted with their 320mm depth along X, which cannot be
right - a shelf's width is also along X, and a shelf spans BETWEEN two
frames. rotateYdeg brings the depth onto Z and the 30mm thickness onto X,
the axis the frames are spaced along.
front: which way the ladder is fitted. After rotateYdeg 90 the ladder runs
x -15..+15, z -160..+160, and the wall-fixing holes are in the z=+160 face -
measured three independent ways, see FINDINGS 'which end faces the wall'.
So the room side is -z, and that is the front.
It is here because every bay was building its SECOND ladder back to front.
A shelf plugs +x at one end and -x at the other; a ladder offers a socket on
BOTH faces of every rung; nothing chose between them, so the solver turned
the far ladder round to make the facings oppose and its wall holes ended up
pointing into the room. Declaring the front is what lets the engine refuse
that placement instead of solving it. Only the frames carry one today - the
rest of the range follows from them, and a front should be measured before
it is declared rather than assumed from the convention.
holes: the two fixings the adjustable foot screws up into, on the frame's
UNDERSIDE. Two 3.40mm full rings at x 0.00, z -119.00 and -81.00 - 38.00mm
apart, fitted to 0.00mm, on all four 320mm frames.
The 200mm frames DO NOT HAVE THEM. Their undersides carry corner radii and
nothing else. That is a product rule, not an omission in the CAD: the foot
only fits a 320mm ladder, so choosing to stand a 200mm bay on feet is a
configuration that cannot be built, and the app now says so rather than
drawing feet that would screw into nothing.
Two masks, not one. The foot's top plate has a round hole one side and a
3mm SLOT the other, and they are different fittings - a bolt that locates
and a bolt that adjusts. Separate masks make each end pair with its own
counterpart, so the foot cannot be fitted 100mm out by matching the wrong
pair. Either connection lands it in the same place, which is the check.
_span: Accessories that span two frames. Each carries a plug at BOTH ends, so the
bay resolves as a chain: frame -> shelf -> frame, with the shelf's width
setting the frame spacing. That is how Kesseboehmer sells it.
The plug sits half a frame thickness in from the part's outer edge, so the
part's end is flush with the frame's outer face. Measured on the 900 shelf:
its end brackets are 29.6mm wide (the frame is 30) centred at x = -460.3,
and half-width minus 15 gives -460.05. Agreement to 0.3mm.
"bearing" says WHICH FACE lands on the rung, and it is not the same across
the family. A shelf is dropped in from above and its bracket's underside is
the part's own base, so bearing is "base" and the plug sits at y = 0 -
verified, the bracket's lowest material lands at exactly 100.0mm with
nothing below it. A clothes rail HANGS below the rung: its 1.5mm top sheet
bears on the same face, so bearing is "top". Get this wrong and the part is
a whole part-height out of place.
The rails' widths agree with the shelves' to within 0.6mm at every size, so
a rail and a shelf ask for the same bay - which they must, or a bay could
not carry both.
008538-41 are the hook strips sold BY LADDER WIDTH, and they belong here
rather than with the hang family. 008536/7 are the ones sold by ladder
DEPTH: those mount depthways on a single frame and hang off it. These span
between two frames exactly like a shelf, which is why the app's hooks looked
wrong with only the depth pair loaded.
Widths measured off the converted geometry: 450 -> 500.2, 600 -> 649.6,
0.0mm, so a bay carries either.
Bearing is "top", and measured rather than reasoned. Counting vertices in
1mm bands down from the top gives the hook strip the same profile as the
clothes rail - dense at 0-2mm, tailing to 3mm, then a gap to 5mm - which is
the 1.5mm top sheet with its bend radius. The rail is already verified at
"top", so the strip presenting an identical sheet settles it.
front: the metal shelves have a RAISED BACK LIP, and it decides which way
they go in. Sliced into 10mm bands along z, all four sizes read identically:
the band at z +114.8..+143.5 reaches y 68.5, the band at -143.5..-114.8 only
reaches 20.0. The tall lip is on the +z side, which is the wall, so the front
is -z - the same answer the ladder gives, arrived at independently.
It matters because a shelf run to the LEFT of a frame mates by its other
plug, and without a front the solver was free to turn the whole shelf round
instead and stand the lip up at the front of the desk. The `run` scenario had
one of those in it.
The clothes rails and the hook strips are NOT given a front here. Both are
asymmetric in z, so both probably have one, but the tall-side test that
settles a shelf says nothing useful about a part that hangs BELOW its rung -
its highest material is the mounting sheet, not a feature you can see. Those
want measuring against the instruction sheets, not guessing.
_wall: Parts that join NOTHING. They are screwed straight to the wall, so they
have no snap planes at all, and their instruction sheets contain no ladder.
The shoe racks are the whole family today. MA 406213 steps 1 and 2 are a
spirit level, a pencil, a drill and wall plugs: 3 holes of 6.5mm, the first
50mm from the end, the rest equally spaced. Lengths 448 / 598 / 898 /
They are sized to the bay and sit inside the composition, which is why they
look attached in the photography. They are not. Matt's call: place them in
space as wall-fixed items so they are there when AR puts the whole thing on
a real wall, rather than pretending they bolt to the ladders.
add-snaps copies these through untouched and writes mounting: "wall" into
the sidecar. That declaration is what makes having no snaps legal - without
it component.js refuses the file with NO_SNAPS, which is the right default
_hang: Accessories that hang on ONE frame and cantilever off it (MA 406209, MA
406210). They lie across the frame's depth, so like the frames they are
converted with their length along X and want the same 90 degree turn.
All of them share one pressed bracket: a 1.5mm top sheet whose underside
bears on the rung's top face, with the obround slot dropping over the rung's
hole and a leg descending just outside the rung's outer face. add-snaps.py
derives the single plug from that slot, so there is no per-part number to
get wrong - only the id, the depth and the turn.
One plug, not two: nothing attaches to the far side of a hung accessory.

hang.minRungBecause: The office desktop assembly fits at rung 3 and above only — Kesseboehmer mark rungs 1 and 2 with a red line.

_youboxx: The YouboXx sets need NO rotation - they come out of CAD with their length
already along Z, unlike every other hang part. Left at 90 they would fail
the slot search rather than silently mount sideways, which is the point of
deriving the plug from the slot instead of a typed-in number.
_notThisSystem: The SHOE RACKS (008553-008556) are not frame accessories at all. MA 406213
screws them straight to a wall with plugs and screws - no ladder appears in
the drawing - and their widths are 448/598/898/1198, the catalogue size
minus 2 rather than the span family's size plus 50. The 6.5mm holes 50mm in
from each end are in the mesh exactly where the drawing dimensions them.
They belong to a wall-fixed product the configurator has no concept of, so
they stay out rather than being forced into a bay.
_notYet: - the clothes rail EXTENSIONS (008533, 008534, 008535). MA 406208 shows a
run over two bays as two tubes sharing a middle bracket, and these parts
carry a bracket at one end only. That is an accessory-to-accessory joint,
a pattern nothing in the engine has needed yet - not just another row.
- the cabinet brackets, office solution, umbrella stand, top panel
bracket, the newspaper-rack divider (it sits in the rack, not on a
frame), the adjustable foot and the wall brackets
Adding the rest is more rows here, not more code.
_collision: `collision` gives a part a handful of boxes that stand in for its shape,
because its own bounding box lies. Only two parts need it and both are
L-sections; everything else in the range is box-shaped enough that its
bounds ARE its shape.
The clamping angle is 20 x 60 x 20 and its box is solid. The real part is a
4mm leg at z -10..-6 running the full height, and a 3mm foot across the top
at y 56..60 lapping forward to z +10. A desktop's back edge sits in the
corner between them - wholly inside the box, touching almost none of the
metal - and the collision survey duly reported both angles as passing
through a desk that was correct.
The office arm is the same story at a bigger size: a 3mm web at x -25..-22
and a 3mm top plate at y 47..50, both running the full 310mm, plus a real
end plate at z -155..-153 that the clamping angle bolts through. Read off
cross-sections of the solid rather than off vertex histograms - a flat
plate has vertices only at its corners, so a histogram shows an L as two
thin bands with a hole in the middle and it is easy to draw the wrong
conclusion.
add-snaps checks two things and refuses the part on either: no box may
stick out past the part, and the boxes TOGETHER must reach the part's own
extremes in all three axes. The second matters more - a proxy that sticks
out is noisy, a part with an uncovered end passes through things silently.
_foot: The adjustable foot 237023, and the first part in the range that is FITTED
AS A CONSEQUENCE rather than chosen. It is not in the palette; it appears
because the mounting option says the bay stands on feet. See implied.js.
It bolts UP into the frame's underside, which is why it is in the `bolted`
family on a +y face rather than being a family of its own. The joint is
vertical, so the solver takes yaw from the product - the same case as the
carcase laid on its brackets - and rotateYdeg 90 is what puts the foot's
50mm plate along the frame's DEPTH before that happens.
Its top plate, measured at y = 99.8: a 5.00mm full ring at x +19.00, and a
3mm SLOT at the other end - two 5.00mm half arcs at x -20.50 and -17.50,
facing apart, centred on -19.00. So the fixings are 38.00mm apart, which is
the frame's 38.00mm to the hundredth. A 90 degree turn puts them at z -19
and z +19, against the frame's z -119 and -81, so the foot lands centred at
z -100 - the front of the frame, which is where the Bedroom photograph and
the foot's own sheet both put it.
The 9.00mm ring at x 0 is the levelling nut, and it is not a fixing. The
sheet gives it +/-10mm of travel; the configurator does not offer that as a
control, because it is set with a spirit level on a real floor.
Height: the mesh is 99.8mm and the SKU is called 100. The 0.2 is real and
is left alone - the product sits 99.8 above the floor in the model and the
quote says 100mm foot, which are both true.
_clampingAngle: Office solution step 4. The clamping angle stands at the REAR end of the
arm and its top foot laps forward over the desktop; step 6 draws a tick and
a cross for whether the board's rear edge is against its upstand or not.
It bolts through a VERTICAL SLOT in the arm's rear end plate - Ø5, x 15,
ends at y 23.0 and y 38.0 - and the slot is there because where the angle
sits depends on how thick the board is.
y 34.5 is that decision for the range's only board, 25mm: the arm carries
at y 51.5 (its own 50 top plus the 1.5 packer), so the board's top is 76.5,
the angle's foot underside is 56.98 up its own leg, and its hole is 14.98
up from its base. 76.5 - 56.98 + 14.98 = 34.5, which is 77% along the slot.
A different board thickness is a different number here, not a different
part - which is exactly what Kesseboehmer put a slot there for.
The slot ends were first written down as 21.75 and 39.25, off by 1.25 at
each end, because find-holes reported each half arc's BOUNDING BOX centre.
